concept.subtitle: The format
concept.title: A race without an end
concept.desc: A Backyard Ultra is a unique ultra-endurance event: no fixed distance, no finish time, just a 6.706 km loop to complete every hour, on the dot.
concept.card1_text: A starting signal is given every hour. All runners still in the race set off together, without exception.
concept.card2_text: Each loop is exactly 6.706 km (4.167 miles). It must be completed within the hour, or you're eliminated.
concept.card3_text: The race continues until only one runner remains able to complete one more loop.
concept.card4_text: Between loops, the base camp brings together runners, crews, and supporters in a friendly, close-knit atmosphere.

ambiance.subtitle: The atmosphere
ambiance.title: Much more than a race
ambiance.card1_text: Between each loop, runners and crews gather in the living area. Tents, deck chairs, homemade food... The atmosphere is unique.
ambiance.card2_text: In a Backyard, runners support one another. You get to know each other hour by hour, encourage one another, share. A sense of community rare in competitive sport.
ambiance.card3_text: An exceptional natural setting: forests, trails, sea air... Brittany offers the perfect backdrop for this ultra-endurance adventure.

header.subtitle: The format
header.title: The Concept of the Backyard Ultra
header.desc: An event invented by Gary Cantrell (aka Lazarus Lake) in 2011, in Tennessee. A unique format that changed the world of ultra-endurance.

principe.subtitle: The principle
principe.desc1_start: The principle of a Backyard is disarmingly simple: complete a loop of
principe.desc1_end: (4.167 miles, or 100 miles after 24h), every single hour, without exception.
principe.desc2: Every new hour, a signal sounds: it's the start. All runners still in the race set off together, whether fresh or exhausted. No individual starts, no exceptions.
principe.desc3_start: If you haven't finished your loop before the next start signal,
principe.desc4_start: The race continues hour after hour, until only one runner remains able to complete one more loop. That runner must then complete this loop
principe.desc4_end: to be declared the official winner. Without that, there is no winner.

cards.km_desc: per loop, every hour, on the dot
cards.c1_text: Each loop must be completed before the next start signal. The clock is always running.
cards.c2_text: If no one can complete one more loop than the others, there is officially no winner.
cards.c3_text: The winner is the last one standing: the one who completes one more loop than everyone else, alone.

schema.subtitle: Understanding the format
schema.title: A race with no scheduled end
schema.desc_start: All runners set off together at the signal.
schema.desc_24h: 24 hours of racing, the equivalent of 100 miles. And it keeps going!
schema.desc_winner: The last one standing completes one extra loop, alone, to claim victory.

rules.r1_text: The signal sounds right on the hour. All runners set off together, regardless of their physical condition.
rules.r2_text: The distance is standardized worldwide. Every Backyard Ultra race uses this same base course.
rules.r3_text: Any runner who has not crossed the finish line before the next start signal is immediately eliminated.
rules.r4_text: To be declared the official winner, the last runner remaining must complete one additional loop, alone.

faq.subtitle: Frequently asked questions
faq.title: Your first questions
faq.q1: What happens if I don't make it within the hour?
faq.a1: You are immediately eliminated. If the next loop's start signal is given before you cross the finish line, you cannot set off again.
faq.q2: How long can a race last?
faq.a2: No one knows in advance! The world record is 124 hours, more than 5 days without stopping. In practice, most races end between 24 and 48 hours.
faq.a3: No. If all runners drop out at the same loop (without a single one managing to complete one more loop than the others), there is no official winner. The winner must always complete one additional loop alone.
faq.a4: Yes! You have a time window (which varies depending on how fast you complete your loop) to rest, eat, tend to injuries... This is where managing your recovery becomes strategic.
faq.q5: Is the format suitable for ultra beginners?
faq.a5: The format is accessible to everyone: there is no technical threshold. But it requires serious mental and physical preparation, as the duration can be very long. We recommend having already run a trail race or a marathon before taking it on.

reglement.title: Rules & Format
reglement.r1: Every hour, on the hour, runners set off on a 6.706 km loop. The first start is at 12:00 PM.
reglement.r2: At the signal, every runner must be in the start corral. Anyone who isn't, or who hasn't finished their loop within the hour, is eliminated.
reglement.r3: Whatever time is left after each loop is yours: rest, eat, change, before the next start.
reglement.r4: The winner is the last runner standing: they must complete one more loop than everyone else, alone. If they can't, there is no winner.
reglement.br1: The bib must be worn visibly at the front throughout the race.
reglement.br2: Any runner dropping out must report it to a member of the organization.
reglement.br3: Your crew can only help you at the base camp, between loops. Any outside help on the course means disqualification.
reglement.br4: The full rules will be shared in the participant pack.

header.subtitle: Help
header.title: Frequently Asked Questions
header.desc: Have questions about the format, the organization, or the race? You'll probably find the answer here.

items.q: What is the Backyard Ultra format?
items.a: A Backyard is an ultra-endurance race format invented by Gary Cantrell (aka Lazarus Lake) in 2011. The principle: complete a 6.706 km loop every hour, until only one runner remains able to complete one more loop.

items.q: Where does the 6.706 km distance come from?
items.a: The exact distance of 6.706 km (or 4.167 miles) comes from a simple mathematical calculation: it allows competitors to cover exactly 100 miles (about 160.9 km) after 24 hours.

items.q: How long can a race last?
items.a: The duration is completely unpredictable. Races lasting less than 10 hours have happened, but the world record is 124 hours (more than 5 days). In practice, the majority of regional races finish between 20 and 40 hours.

No, only one official winner is possible. If several runners drop out at the same loop, or if the last remaining runner cannot complete the extra solo loop, there is no official winner for that edition.

It's the original race, created by Lazarus Lake in Bell Buckle, Tennessee (USA). It now hosts the Backyard Ultra Individual World Championship in odd years: about 75 runners qualify, the national champions (the "Golden Ticket", with at least 24 loops) and the best performances worldwide over the previous two years. In even years comes the Team World Championship: each country holds its national race on the same day, with a team of 15 runners.
Registration for the next edition is not yet open. Sign up for our newsletter to be notified first as soon as it opens.
The number of spots will be announced when registration opens. The Backyard Ultra format works best with a moderate number of participants: expect limited spots.

items.q: Is there a minimum required level?
items.a: There is no mandatory technical qualification, but we recommend having trail running or long-distance racing experience (marathon minimum). The format is very demanding, both physically and mentally.
The refund policy will be specified when registration opens. Cancellation terms will be stated in the rulebook.

The essentials: trail running shoes, a headlamp, weather-appropriate clothing, and your own food supplies. For the base camp: a tent or shelter, a deck chair, a sleeping bag, and spare clothing. See the 'Practical Info' page for the full list.

items.q: Can I have a support crew?
items.a: Yes! Your crew can be present in the living area throughout the race. However, they cannot assist you on the course itself.
Yes, walking / trekking poles are allowed throughout the race.

items.q: Are there showers or restrooms on site?
items.a: Restrooms will be available in the living area. Full details will be provided in the participant pack.

The organization provides a continuous supply of drinking water, fresh fruit (bananas, oranges) between loops, hot broth at night, and coffee/tea. Full aid station details will be provided in the rulebook.

items.q: Can I bring my own food?
items.a: Yes, and it's strongly recommended! You know better than anyone what works for you during long efforts. Avoid any food you haven't tested in training.

items.q: Is there an aid station on the course?
items.a: No. The only aid station is at the living area, at the start/finish. You'll have the remaining time after each loop to refuel before the next start.
The race continues around the clock, including at night. The course is marked with reflective tape. A headlamp is mandatory after nightfall.
Yes! If you finish your loop in 45 minutes, you have 15 minutes to rest. Some runners use alarms for 10-12 minute micro-naps. This is one of the key tactics of the format.

The Breizh Backyard is organised by the Delta Events association. We are 4 young people passionate about running and trail, driven by the desire to create a unique ultra-endurance event in Brittany. It's a 100% non-profit project, fuelled by the passion and energy of our team.

items.q: What does the entry fee cover?
items.a: The entire entry fee is reinvested into organising the event: logistics, course marking, aid stations, insurance, and equipment. Our team is 100% volunteer and, as a non-profit association, we make no profit: every euro goes towards giving you the best possible experience.

items.q: How can I contact the organisation?
items.a: Feel free to reach out via our Contact page or directly by email. Whether it's a question, a suggestion, or a partnership enquiry, we're happy to respond to every message!
